subject: physics_2
question_text: What do you understand by resonance? How would you use resonance to determine the velocity of sound in air?

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it — the figure carries 0 marks because the question does not ask for a diagram. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: a closed air column resonates at l₁ = λ/4 and again at l₂ = 3λ/4, so l₂ − l₁ = λ/2 and λ = 2(l₂ − l₁); with V = nλ this gives V = 2n(l₂ − l₁). The relation l₂ = 3l₁ holds only for an ideal tube with no end correction, so the card does not print it: in a real tube l₁ = λ/4 − e and l₂ = 3λ/4 − e, and using the difference of the two lengths cancels that end correction.

recall_prompt: Say what resonance is, then the two resonating lengths of the air column and how they give the velocity of sound.

steps.label: Resonance defined

An air column vibrating like this with a
tuning fork is a resonating air column.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both phrases matter: equals the natural frequency, and maximum amplitude.
steps.why: The definition needs the matching condition (external frequency = natural frequency) AND the observable result (maximum amplitude) — the experiment below detects resonance by exactly that loud maximum.
common_mistakes: Writing large amplitude instead of maximum amplitude — resonance is the peak response, not just a big one.
Leaving out the natural frequency — without the matching condition the sentence describes any forced vibration.

recall.must_convey: That resonance is maximum-amplitude vibration when the forcing frequency equals the body's natural frequency.
accept: external frequency equals the natural frequency
the body vibrates with maximum amplitude
a resonating air column with a tuning fork
reject: first resonance at lambda by four

steps.memory_tip: Match the frequency, get the maximum — the two halves of the definition.

steps.label: The air column at two lengths
steps.margin_note: No marks ride on the figure, but drawing the two column lengths makes the λ/4 and 3λ/4 claims visible.
steps.why: The two sketches fix the geometry the working uses: the closed (water) end is always a node and the open end an antinode, so the shortest resonating column is a quarter wave and the next is three quarters.
common_mistakes: Drawing an antinode at the closed end — the closed end cannot move, so it is always a node.

recall.must_convey: That the sketch shows the air column resonating at l₁ = λ/4 and again at l₂ = 3λ/4.
accept: draw the column at the two resonating lengths
node at the closed end, antinode at the open end
reject: V equals two n times the length difference

steps.memory_tip: Closed end: node. Open end: antinode. The first two fits are λ/4 and 3λ/4.

steps.label: The two resonating lengths
lines: A vibrating tuning fork of frequency n is
held over a closed air column whose
length can be changed. The length is
increased until the sound is loudest —
the column resonates with the fork.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two loudest lengths, and their λ values.
steps.why: A closed column resonates when a node sits at the closed end and an antinode at the open end; the shortest such fit is a quarter wavelength and the next fit adds half a wavelength — that is where λ/4 and 3λ/4 come from.
common_mistakes: Writing the second resonance as λ/2 — the next fit for a CLOSED column is 3λ/4; λ/2 belongs to open pipes.
Detecting resonance by anything but the loudest sound — maximum loudness IS the resonance signal.

recall.must_convey: That the column resonates first at l₁ = λ/4 and next at l₂ = 3λ/4.
accept: first resonance at lambda by four
second at three lambda by four
raise the column till the sound is loudest
reject: lambda equals two l two minus l one

steps.memory_tip: The column grows by half a wavelength between one resonance and the next: λ/4, then 3λ/4.

steps.label: Wavelength from the two lengths
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The difference of the two lengths gives half a wavelength.
steps.why: Using the DIFFERENCE of two measured lengths, instead of l₁ alone, cancels the small end correction of the tube — both lengths carry the same error and subtraction removes it.
common_mistakes: Writing λ = 4l₁ and stopping — correct in principle but the method asks for both lengths; the difference is the measured quantity.
Forgetting the factor 2 — the difference is λ/2, so λ is twice the difference.

recall.must_convey: That l₂ − l₁ = λ/2, so λ = 2(l₂ − l₁).
accept: the difference is half a wavelength
lambda is twice l two minus l one

steps.memory_tip: Between resonances the column grew by exactly half a wave — double the growth to get λ.

steps.label: Velocity of sound
lines: With the wave relation V = nλ, where n is
the frequency of the tuning fork:
Measuring l₁ and l₂ for a fork of known
frequency gives the velocity of sound in
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Substitute λ into V = nλ and box the result.
steps.why: The fork's frequency is stamped on it and the two lengths are read off the apparatus, so every quantity on the right side is measured — the formula turns the experiment into a number for V.
common_mistakes: Using the frequency of the air column instead of the fork — at resonance they are equal, and the KNOWN one is the fork's.
Writing V = n(l₂ − l₁) — the difference is λ/2, so the 2 must appear.

recall.must_convey: That V = nλ = 2n(l₂ − l₁), with n the tuning fork frequency.
accept: V equals two n times l two minus l one
substitute lambda into V equals n lambda
reject: the difference is half a wavelength

steps.memory_tip: Known fork frequency × measured wavelength — the whole experiment sits inside V = nλ.

insider_note: The examiner looks for the pair λ/4 and 3λ/4 and the final V = 2n(l₂ − l₁) — the difference form matters because it is the measured version, not the memorised one.
